title: Rights and tax money: what India's laws promise every family

summary.text: Almost every bill from a shop or restaurant has a line called GST. That is tax, money paid to the government with every purchase. So the books, roads and street lights we call 'free' are paid for by all of us together. A right is something the law promises every person. India's laws promise every child aged 6 to 14 a free school place. They promise every citizen the right to ask how public money is spent. They promise rural families paid work when they need it. In this unit you hunt for the tax on your own family's bills, check a pretend work register for cheating, and find out where the things in your home were made.
summary.art: A child at a dining table holding a long supermarket bill up to the light, one line circled in pencil, with faint pictures behind of a school, a street light and a road.

intro.hook: Pick up a school textbook or a printed bill. A government school gives that book free. A shop bill has a small line called GST. Is the free book really free? Who paid for it?
intro.text: The book was paid for with public money. Public money is the money the government collects from people, mostly as tax. Some of it came from the GST on bills like yours. In this unit you find out how much tax your family pays when it shops. Then you learn three laws that come from this idea. Every child has a right to go to school. Every citizen has a right to know how public money is spent. Every rural family has a right to ask for paid work.
intro.art: A plain school textbook lying next to a supermarket bill, with a pencil arrow drawn from the GST line on the bill to the book.

outcomes: I can find the tax on a bill, and explain that almost everyone pays tax when they buy things.
I can explain what a right is, and name three rights India's laws give: school, information and work.
I can say what the Right to Education Act promises children aged 6 to 14.
I can explain why any citizen may ask how public money is spent, and how to write a Right to Information question.
I can explain what the rural job guarantee promises village families, and how a social audit checks it.
I can find where things at home were made, and give one good side and one worry about trade with the whole world.
I can give two sides of a real argument about these laws, using evidence.

terms.meaning: The government is the group of people chosen to run the country, a state or a town for everyone. In India, people vote to choose them.
terms.example: The Tamil Nadu government runs the state's government schools and buses.
terms.art: A big building with many windows and a flag on top, with a queue of people walking in.

terms.meaning: A law is a rule for the whole country or state. Everyone must follow it, including the government. A law made by Parliament is called an Act.
terms.example: The law says a car must stop at a red light.
terms.art: A thick book with a ribbon marker lying open on a table.

terms.meaning: The Constitution is India's most important law. It says how the country is run and what rights every person has. It came into force on 26 January 1950.
terms.example: We celebrate Republic Day on 26 January because the Constitution began that day.
terms.art: A large handwritten book with a decorated border, open on a stand.

terms.meaning: A right is something every person is allowed to have or do, and the law protects it. Nobody has to earn it or pay for it.
terms.example: Every child aged 6 to 14 in India has the right to a free school place.
terms.art: A girl with a school bag walking through an open school gate.

terms.meaning: Tax is money people must pay to the government. The government uses it to pay for things everyone shares, such as roads, schools and hospitals.
terms.example: When you buy a packet of biscuits, a little of the price is tax.
terms.art: A one-rupee coin dropping from a shopping bag into a big shared pot.

terms.meaning: GST stands for Goods and Services Tax. It is the tax added to the price of most things we buy in India. A bill often shows it as CGST and SGST. Half goes to the central government and half to the state.
terms.example: A restaurant bill for a plate of dosa shows a few rupees of CGST and the same of SGST.
terms.art: A shop bill with two lines underlined: CGST and SGST.

terms.meaning: Public money is money the government holds for everyone. Most of it comes from tax. It is spent on things that belong to all of us.
terms.example: The street light outside your building was paid for with public money.
terms.art: A street light glowing at dusk over a road, with a small rupee sign on its pole.

terms.meaning: This law, passed in 2009, says every child aged 6 to 14 must get a free school place, up to Class 8. Schools may not test small children before giving them a seat.
terms.example: A 6-year-old in Madurai joins Class 1 at a government school without paying any fee.
terms.art: A small boy in a uniform holding his mother's hand at a school gate, a teacher smiling.

terms.meaning: This law, passed in 2005, lets any citizen ask a government office for information. The office must answer within 30 days. People call it RTI.
terms.example: A family in Kochi asks the town office how much the repair of their road cost.
terms.art: A hand dropping a letter into a box labelled 'RTI applications'.

terms.meaning: The Public Information Officer is the person in each government office whose job is to answer RTI questions.
terms.example: A letter about the road repair goes to the Public Information Officer of the town office.
terms.art: A woman officer at a desk reading a letter, with a stack of files beside her.

terms.meaning: This is a law that promises paid work to village families who ask for it, on jobs like digging ponds. From 2006 it was called MGNREGA and promised 100 days a year. From 1 July 2026, a new law promises 125 days.
terms.example: In a village near Anantapur, women dig a farm pond and are paid by the day.
terms.art: Village women with baskets and spades digging a pond under a hot sky.

terms.meaning: A job card is a small book given free to a village family that wants work under the job guarantee. It records the days each person worked and the wages paid.
terms.example: Ratnamma's job card shows she worked 12 days on the pond in March.
terms.art: A small booklet with a family photo on the cover and a table of dates inside.

terms.meaning: A muster roll is the attendance list at a work site. It shows who worked on which days, so they can be paid.
terms.example: The muster roll for the pond has 6 names and a tick for each day each person came.
terms.art: A long paper register with names down the side and ticks in boxes.

terms.meaning: A social audit is a meeting where the work records are read aloud in the village. The people who did the work say whether the records are true.
terms.example: At the social audit, a worker stands up and says, 'I worked 10 days, not 6.'
terms.art: A village meeting under a big tree, a woman reading from a register to a crowd.

terms.meaning: Transparency means being open, so anyone can see how decisions are made and money is spent. Glass is transparent because you can see through it.
terms.example: A board at a building site shows the work's cost and the date it will finish.
terms.art: A glass box with coins inside, and people looking in from all sides.

terms.meaning: Globalisation means the countries of the world becoming more connected through trade, travel, jobs and the internet.
terms.example: A phone with parts from many countries is put together in Chennai and sold in Kenya.
terms.art: A globe with thin lines joining many cities, a ship and an aeroplane on the lines.

terms.meaning: An import is something brought into India from another country to sell. An export is something made in India and sold to another country.
terms.example: India exports rice and medicines. India imports oil and many electronic parts.
terms.art: A cargo ship being loaded with sacks of rice at a port.

explanations.definition: A right is something every person may have or do, which the law protects. A person does not have to earn it or pay for it.
explanations.description: India's Constitution lists Fundamental Rights, such as being equal before the law and speaking freely. Parliament can also make laws that give new rights. A right is different from a gift. A gift can be taken back when the giver changes their mind. A right stays, and if an office refuses it, a person can complain or go to court. Rights also come with work for someone. A child's right to school means the government must build schools and pay teachers.
examples: Every child aged 6 to 14 has the right to a free school place.
Every citizen has the right to ask a government office for information.
Every person has the right to be treated equally by the law, whatever their religion, caste or whether they are a girl or a boy.
explanations.art: A row of people of different ages standing in a line, each holding the same small book with a ribbon.
explanations.context: This card says what a right is, and how it is different from a gift.

explanations.definition: Tax is money people must pay to the government. Public money is what the government collects, mostly from tax, to spend on things everyone shares.
explanations.description: Most people never hand money straight to the government. They pay tax inside the price of what they buy. GST began in India on 1 July 2017. Since 22 September 2025, most goods carry GST of 5% or 18%. That means 5 or 18 rupees for every 100 rupees of price. Some things, such as fresh vegetables, carry none. People who earn more also pay income tax. So a family that only buys rice, soap and a bus ticket is still paying tax. This is why the government's money is really the people's money.
examples: A bill shows CGST 2.5% and SGST 2.5%. That adds up to 5 rupees of tax on every 100 rupees of price.
The road, the drain, the bus stop and the government hospital are paid for with public money.
A small kirana shop's handwritten slip often shows no GST. Very small shops do not have to collect it.
explanations.art: A bill turning into coins that flow into a big pot, and from the pot into a school, a road and a hospital.
explanations.context: This card explains tax, and why the government's money comes from almost every family.

explanations.concept: The right to go to school
explanations.definition: Under the Right to Education Act, 2009, every child aged 6 to 14 has the right to free school up to Class 8, in a school near home.
explanations.description: For a long time, millions of children in India did not go to school. Many had to work, or had no school nearby. In 2002, the Constitution was changed to make free school a Fundamental Right for children aged 6 to 14. The Right to Education Act came into force on 1 April 2010. It says government schools must not charge fees. A school may not hold a test before giving a small child a seat, or ask for a donation. A child must not be turned away for having no birth certificate. A teacher must not hit or frighten a child. Private schools must keep a quarter of the seats in their first class for children from poor families, and the government pays for those seats.
examples: A school in Hyderabad asks a 5-year-old to sit an entry test. The law does not allow this.
A private school in Mysuru keeps 25 of its 100 first-class seats for children from poor families.
A girl whose family moved from Odisha to Chennai is given a seat though she has no birth certificate.
explanations.art: A teacher writing on a blackboard while children of many backgrounds sit together on mats in a bright classroom.
explanations.context: This card explains the Right to Education Act: what it promises children and what schools may not do.

explanations.definition: Government schools in India give children a free cooked lunch on school days. The scheme is now called PM POSHAN.
explanations.description: A hungry child finds it hard to learn, and a free lunch brings many children to school. Madras, now Chennai, began giving lunch to poor school children about a hundred years ago. In the 1950s, the government of Madras State, led by K. Kamaraj, spread free lunches across the state. In 2001, India's Supreme Court ordered every government primary school in the country to serve a cooked lunch. Since 2022, Tamil Nadu also gives a free breakfast in its government primary schools.
examples: A Class 3 child in a government school in Madurai eats rice, sambar and an egg at lunch.
Studies have found that more girls come to school when lunch is served.
explanations.art: Children sitting in a long row on a school verandah with steel plates, as a cook serves rice and sambar.
explanations.context: This card is about the free lunch in government schools, and where the idea began.

explanations.definition: Under the Right to Information Act, 2005, any citizen may ask a government office for information, and the office must answer within 30 days.
explanations.description: The money a government office spends came from the people, so the people may ask how it was spent. The person asking does not need to give a reason. They write a short letter to the office's Public Information Officer, in English, Hindi or the state's language. The fee is 10 rupees for central government offices, and families below the poverty line pay nothing. States set their own fees. If the question is about someone's life or freedom, the answer must come within 48 hours. If an officer delays without good reason, they can be fined. Some things may be kept secret, such as information that would harm the country's safety or a person's private life. Tamil Nadu and Goa made state laws like this in 1997. The law for the whole country came into force on 12 October 2005.
examples: A mother in Chennai asks the city corporation when the broken street light outside her building will be fixed.
Villagers ask how much money was spent on their school's new toilet, and who built it.
A student asks the university for a copy of their own marked answer sheet.
explanations.art: A woman posting a letter at a post office counter, with a calendar behind her showing 30 days circled.
explanations.context: This card explains the Right to Information Act: who may ask, how to ask, and how soon the answer must come.

explanations.definition: A rural job guarantee is a law that promises paid manual work to any village family whose adults ask for it.
explanations.description: In many villages, there is little paid work in the months between harvests. Many people then leave for cities to look for jobs. India's National Rural Employment Guarantee Act was passed in 2005. Its first work began on 2 February 2006, in Bandlapalli village in Anantapur district, Andhra Pradesh. In 2009 it was renamed after Mahatma Gandhi and became MGNREGA. It promised every village household up to 100 days of paid work a year. A family asks the Gram Panchayat, the elected village council. They get a free job card. If no work is given within 15 days, the family must be paid an allowance. Women and men get the same wage, and wages go into a bank or post office account. A work site must have drinking water, shade and first aid. On 1 July 2026, a new law, the VB-G RAM G Act, replaced MGNREGA. It promises up to 125 days of work a year.
examples: Women in a Telangana village dig a farm pond, so rainwater stays for the dry months.
A family in Kerala asks the Gram Panchayat for work and gets a dated receipt for their request.
Workers build a small check dam across a stream, so the water soaks into the ground.
explanations.art: Village women and men carrying baskets of earth from a half-dug pond, with a small shaded shelter and a water pot nearby.
explanations.context: This card explains the rural job guarantee: what it promised village families, and how it changed in 2026.

explanations.description: When records are kept shut in an office, a dishonest person can write a false name or false days, and nobody notices. When the records are read aloud to the people they are about, the false parts stand out. A worker knows how many days she worked. A villager knows whether a road was really built. That is why the job guarantee law requires a social audit, where the village checks the records. Andhra Pradesh was one of the first states to hold regular social audits of the job scheme, from 2006. Many studies have found that open records reduce cheating. They do not stop it completely, and researchers still argue about how much they help.
examples: A muster roll shows a man working 12 days, but he was in Hyderabad all month. The villagers know, and say so at the meeting.
A board at a building site lists the cost of the work, so anyone passing can ask questions.
explanations.art: A register lying open on a table in the middle of a village meeting, many hands pointing at one line.
explanations.context: This card explains why reading records aloud to the people they are about helps catch mistakes and cheating.

explanations.description: A phone, a toy or a cooking oil may come from far away. Ships, aeroplanes and the internet have made trade between countries fast and cheap. This is a big part of globalisation. In 1991, India made new rules that opened it up much more to world trade. India now exports rice, medicines, cars, clothes and computer services. It imports oil, gold and many electronic parts. Many things are made in steps across many countries. A 'Made in' label names only where the thing was finished. People agree that trade has made many things cheaper. They argue about who gains and who loses.
examples: Tomatoes, potatoes and chillies first came to India from the Americas, about 500 years ago. Now they feel completely Indian.
Many phones sold in India are now put together in factories near Chennai and in Noida, from parts made in many countries.
A handloom weaver in Kanchipuram sells silk saris to buyers in other countries.

perspectives.explanation: Since India opened up to trade in 1991, it has grown faster, and far fewer people live in deep poverty. Trade brings cheaper goods and new jobs in factories and offices.

Gandhi asked Indians to use things made close to home, such as khadi cloth, because machine-made cloth from Britain had ruined many Indian weavers. People in this tradition say cheap imports still put local makers out of work, and shipping goods across the world burns a lot of fuel.

explanations.art: A globe with a phone, a sack of rice, a silk sari and a bottle of oil around it, each joined to a different country by a dotted line.
explanations.context: This card is about trade between countries, and the real argument about whether it helps everyone.

explanations.description: The rural job guarantee was one of the biggest work schemes in the world. People who study it agree on some things. It gave many poor families money in the hardest months, and more than half its workdays went to women. They also agree that wages were often paid late, and some money was stolen with false names. They disagree about how much good it did overall, and about the new law of 2026.
examples: In a drought year, a family's job card wages pay for food until the rains come.
A study in Andhra Pradesh found that paying wages with smart cards, checked by fingerprint, reduced stealing.

perspectives.who: The economist Jean Drèze, who helped write the 2005 law
perspectives.explanation: The law gave poor families a right, not a favour. They could demand work and be paid. It stopped many people from going hungry in bad years.
A lot of money was wasted or stolen, and some of the work built little of lasting use. The money might help more if it were spent in other ways, such as on roads or training.
The new law gives more days, but states must now pay a bigger share of the cost, and there is a fixed budget. They worry that poorer states will offer less work.

explanations.art: A balance scale with a sack of rice and a happy family on one side, and a late-payment notice and a torn register on the other.
explanations.context: This card is about a real argument: how well India's rural job guarantee worked.

agreed.text: Almost everyone in India pays tax, because GST is added to the price of most things people buy.
agreed.evidence: GST appears on the printed bills of shops, restaurants and online orders. You can check your own family's bills.

agreed.text: Since 2010, every child in India aged 6 to 14 has had a legal right to free school up to Class 8.
agreed.evidence: The Right to Education Act, 2009, and Article 21A of the Constitution, added in 2002.

agreed.text: Any Indian citizen may ask a government office for information, and does not have to give a reason.
agreed.evidence: The Right to Information Act, 2005. Lakhs of people use it every year.

agreed.text: Reading work records aloud to the workers helps catch false entries.
agreed.evidence: The public hearings of the MKSS in Rajasthan in the 1990s, and the regular social audits held in states such as Andhra Pradesh.

challenging.claim: Things the government gives, such as school books and lunches, are free.
challenging.for: The family does not pay anything at the school gate.
challenging.against: They are paid for with public money, and most of that comes from tax that almost every family pays when it shops. Nobody pays at the gate, but everyone has paid already.
challenging.context: This card is about a common idea: that what the government gives costs nothing.

challenging.who: A common idea, among children and grown-ups
challenging.for: Rich people pay income tax, and poor people mostly do not.
challenging.against: GST is in the price of most things anyone buys, so a poor family that buys soap or oil pays tax too.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that only rich people pay tax.

challenging.claim: The government's records must be true, because they are official.
challenging.who: Many people, before the right to information campaigns
challenging.for: Records are written by trained officers and signed and stamped.
challenging.against: Public hearings in Rajasthan in the 1990s found records of payments to workers who were never paid, and of works that were never built.
challenging.context: This card is about whether official records can always be trusted.

challenging.claim: Trade with other countries makes everyone better off.
challenging.for: Trade has made phones, clothes and many other things much cheaper, and India's exports have created many jobs.
challenging.against: Some people lose their work when cheaper goods come from far away, such as weavers and toy makers. The gains are not shared equally.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument: does trade help everyone?

challenging.claim: Too many RTI questions slow the government down.
challenging.for: Answering lakhs of questions takes officers' time, and some questions are asked only to trouble an officer.
challenging.against: Many offices now put information online before anyone asks, which saves time. Supporters say the questions catch waste worth far more than the time spent.
challenging.context: This card is about a real argument over the Right to Information Act.

big_questions.q: If almost everyone pays tax, who should decide how it is spent?
big_questions.hint: Think about voting, and about the RTI letter. Is voting once every five years enough, or should people be able to ask questions in between?

big_questions.q: A right needs someone to do work, such as a teacher for the right to school. If nobody does that work, does the right still exist?
big_questions.hint: Think of a village school with no teacher. The law says the children have a right to learn. What is missing?

big_questions.q: Why did a list of names read aloud in a village catch cheating that officers in offices missed?
big_questions.hint: Who knows best how many days a worker worked?

big_questions.q: Is it better to buy a cheaper thing from far away, or a costlier one made by someone in your own town?
big_questions.hint: Think about the price, the maker, the fuel used to carry it, and what you would want to know before deciding.

big_questions.q: A label says 'Made in India', but the parts came from five countries. Where was the thing really made?
big_questions.hint: Think of a dosa. The rice, urad dal and salt came from different places. Where was the dosa made?

big_questions.q: Should children have a say in how their school is run?
big_questions.hint: The Right to Education Act asks every government school to have a School Management Committee of parents and teachers. Who is missing from it?

story.title: The Name on the List
story.note: Social audits of the rural job guarantee are real: the Gram Sabha meets, a social audit team reads out the muster rolls, and workers say whether they are true. Andhra Pradesh held them regularly from 2006. Lakshmi, her family, Sujatha and this village are made up.
text: Lakshmi was eight, and she lived in a village of red earth and groundnut fields near Anantapur, in Andhra Pradesh. She was in Class 3 at the government school. She liked school lunch, and she liked reading more than anything.

Her grandmother, Ammamma Ratnamma, could not read. When Ammamma was small, there was no school near the village, and girls were kept at home to fetch water. Now, every summer, Ammamma dug earth for the new farm pond with the other women of the village. The work was paid under the job guarantee. Ammamma kept her job card wrapped in a plastic cover, inside the rice tin, so the rats could not eat it.

Lakshmi's uncle, Ravi Mama, did not dig the pond. He had gone to Hyderabad in March to work as a mason on a tall building. Every Sunday evening he called on the phone. He told Lakshmi how many floors the building had grown that week.
One morning in May, a jeep stopped near the panchayat office. A woman got out with a bag full of papers. Her name was Sujatha, and she led the social audit team.
'What is a social audit?' Lakshmi asked her teacher.

'It is a checking meeting,' said her teacher, Mrs Fathima. 'The team has copied the records of the pond work. Tomorrow they will read them aloud to the whole village. The workers will say if they are true.'
'Why read them aloud?' asked Lakshmi. 'Can't the officers just check them in the office?'
'The officers can check that the sums add up,' said Mrs Fathima. 'But only the workers know if they really worked on those days.'

The next afternoon, the whole village sat under the big neem tree. Men sat on one side and women on the other, and children sat in front, in the dust. Sujatha stood with a long register, the muster roll. It listed every worker's name, with a tick for each day they came.
She read slowly, in Telugu. 'Ratnamma. Twelve days in April. Paid for twelve days.'

Ammamma frowned. She leaned over and whispered to Lakshmi. Lakshmi took the job card out of its plastic cover and counted the stamped days. 'Fifteen,' she whispered back. 'Ammamma worked fifteen days.'
Ammamma stood up. Her voice shook a little, because she had never spoken in a meeting before. 'I worked fifteen days, not twelve. My job card says so.'
Sujatha checked the card and wrote a note. 'Three days are missing,' she said. 'Ratnamma garu must be paid for three more days.' A few women clapped.
Sujatha read on, name after name. Then she read, 'Ravi. Twelve days in April. Paid for twelve days.'
Lakshmi sat up very straight. Ravi Mama had been in Hyderabad all of April. He had told her about the building every Sunday. He could not have dug the pond.
Her heart was thumping. Everyone would look at her. But it was true, and she knew it. She raised her hand.
'Ravi Mama was not here in April,' she said. 'He was working in Hyderabad. He called us every Sunday from there.'
The crowd went quiet. Then an old man said, 'That's right. Ravi left before Ugadi.' A woman said, 'I never saw him at the pond.'

Sujatha looked at the worksite helper, the mate, who kept the muster roll. He looked at his feet. At last he said that he had added some names of people who were away. The wages for those days had gone into an account he could use.

Sujatha wrote it all down. 'This will go to the officers,' she said. 'The money must be paid back.' Then she turned to Lakshmi. 'Thank you. The register looked perfect in the office. It took someone who knew the truth to find the mistake.'
That night, Ravi Mama called from Hyderabad. Lakshmi told him everything. He laughed, and then he went quiet.
'So someone used my name for money,' he said. 'And my niece caught them.'
Ammamma was rolling chapatis by the stove. 'Tomorrow,' she said, 'you will teach me to read the job card myself.'
Lakshmi got out her slate. She wrote a large R and a T, the first letters of Ratnamma in English. Ammamma copied them carefully, her tongue between her teeth.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the muster roll looked correct in the office, because its sums added up. The mistakes showed only when the record was read to the people it was about. Ammamma knew her own days, and Lakshmi knew where her uncle had been. This is why the job guarantee law requires social audits, and why the Right to Information Act matters: a record can be checked only by people who are allowed to see it. Lakshmi could help because she could read, which is what the Right to Education Act is for. And the wages, the school and the audit were all paid for with public money, from the tax that families like Lakshmi's pay.
ask: Why did the officers in the office not notice that Ravi's name was wrong?
How did Lakshmi know that Ravi Mama was not at the pond?
Ammamma's voice shook when she stood up. Why do you think it was hard for her to speak?
How did Lakshmi being able to read help her family and her village?
Who do you think should check the records of work done near your home?

items.f: Aditi's shoes say Made in Vietnam. She asks why.
items.b: Globalisation. Countries trade, so things made far away are sold here.

items.f: A toy maker in Channapatna sells fewer wooden toys since cheap plastic toys arrived.
items.b: Globalisation. Trade brings cheaper goods, but some local makers lose work.

Then they say exactly what the caller should do. That earns 1 more point.
Turn the card over to check. If the answer is different, talk about why.
Take turns being the helpline worker. After 16 calls, the most points wins. Playing alone, try to get 24 points out of 32.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 16 cards. 2. Shuffle them. 3. Put them face down in a pile.

flow.say: Ring ring! Hello, is this the rights helpline? Here is my problem.
flow.kid: Listen to the caller. Which law helps? What should they do? Then check the back.
flow.parent: Read the cards in a worried caller's voice. It helps your child picture a real person. If your child names the law but not what to do, ask: 'Who should I write to? What should I say?'

flow.say: Which call was the hardest to answer? Which of these laws do you think helps the most people, and why?
flow.kid: Which call was hardest? Which law helps the most people? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Which law do you think helps the most people?
good: The Right to Education, because every child goes to school.
The Right to Information, because anyone can use it.
Any answer with a reason.

experiments.title: The Bill Detective: how much of what we pay is tax?
experiments.context: In this experiment you look at real bills from your family's shopping. You find the tax on each one, and work out how many rupees of every 100 went to the government.
experiments.question: Does every bill have tax on it? For every 100 rupees of price, how many rupees go to the government?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Will every bill have tax on it, or only some? For every 100 rupees of price, how many rupees do you think are tax: 1, 5, 20 or 50? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Look at every bill in the same way: find the total, find each tax line, and find the rate printed beside it. Use at least 5 bills from different kinds of shop, because one bill could be unusual.
results_table: Rupees of tax in every 100 of price

materials.item: 5 to 8 printed bills from different places: a supermarket, a medical shop, a restaurant, a sweet shop, a hardware shop. An online order's invoice on a phone also works.
a handwritten slip from a small kirana shop or vegetable seller, if you have one
a notebook, a pencil and a highlighter or coloured pencil

schedule.what: Collect the bills. Guess how much is tax. Find the tax on each bill. Sort them, and talk about where the tax goes.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for every bill. Circle the bill with the most tax for every 100 rupees, and the bill with none.

flow.do: 1. Spread the bills on a table. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guess at the top of the page.
flow.say: These are bills from our shopping. Before we look closely, guess. Will every bill have tax on it? Out of every 100 rupees, how much is tax? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the bills. Guess: does every bill have tax? How much in every 100 rupees? Write your guess.

good: Because the price already looks right, so tax must be small.
Because I saw GST on a bill before.
Any reason is good. We will test it.

flow.parent: Children often guess there is no tax at all, or that tax is half the price. Both are fine. Do not tell them the answer yet. Before you start, cover any card or phone numbers with a strip of paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Bill Detective. You guess how much of each bill is tax before you look.

flow.do: 1. Take one bill. 2. Find the total and write it in the table. 3. Find the lines called CGST and SGST, or IGST, or GST. 4. Highlight them and add them up. 5. Do the same for every bill.
flow.say: Tax on a bill usually hides near the bottom. Look for the letters GST. If there are two lines, CGST and SGST, add them together.
flow.kid: Find the total on each bill. Then hunt for GST near the bottom. Add CGST and SGST together. Write the tax.
flow.parent: CGST goes to the central government and SGST to the state. They are usually equal. Some supermarket bills show a small tax table at the bottom, sorted by rate. Add up the tax column. A handwritten slip usually has no GST at all. That is a real result, so write 0.

flow.do: 1. Look beside each tax line for a percent sign, such as 2.5% or 9%. 2. Add the two rates together. 3. Write it as rupees of tax in every 100 rupees of price.
flow.say: The rate tells you how many rupees of tax are added to every 100 rupees of price. 2.5% and 2.5% make 5 rupees in every 100.
flow.kid: Find the numbers with a percent sign. Add the two together. That is tax in every 100 rupees.
flow.parent: Percent means 'out of every hundred'. Your child does not need to calculate it, only to add the two printed rates. 9% and 9% make 18 rupees in every 100. If a bill has items at two rates, write both. Since September 2025, most things carry 5% or 18% in all.

check.q: A bill shows CGST 9% and SGST 9%. How many rupees of tax are added to every 100 rupees of price?
check.why: The two taxes are added together: 9 for the central government and 9 for the state, so 18 rupees in every 100. Picking 9 means you counted only one of the two taxes.

flow.do: 1. Put the bills in a line from the most tax in every 100 to the least. 2. Find any bill with no tax. 3. Talk about why.
flow.say: Line up the bills from the most tax to the least. Which bill had none? Why might that be?
flow.kid: Line up the bills. Most tax first. Which bill had no tax? Why?

ask.q: Why might the vegetable seller's slip have no tax?
good: Fresh vegetables carry no GST.
Very small shops don't have to collect it.

ask.q: Which bills had the most tax?
good: Things like plastic goods, electronics or paint often carry 18%.
Food and medicines mostly carry 5%.

flow.parent: Most food and medicine bills show 5% in all. Many other goods show 18%. Loose fresh vegetables, fruit and loose grain carry none. Very small shops do not have to collect GST.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to say the claim, the evidence and the reason. 2. Then ask where the tax goes.
flow.say: So what did you find? Say what you think, what you saw on the bills, and why. Then tell me: where does all this tax money go?
flow.kid: Say what you found. Say which bills showed it. Where does the tax money go?

ask.q: Who paid tax this week in our family?
good: We all did, when we bought things.
Anyone who went shopping.

ask.q: Where does the tax money go?
good: To the government.
It pays for roads, schools, hospitals and street lights.

flow.think: If your family's money helped pay for the road, should you be allowed to ask how it was spent?

experiments.title: Made Where? A home survey of 20 things
experiments.context: In this experiment you check 20 things in your home for a 'Made in' label. You find out how many were made in India and how many came from other countries.
experiments.question: Out of 20 things in our home, how many were made in India, and how many in other countries?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Out of 20 things, how many will be made in India? Which other country will appear most often? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Choose 20 things before you look at any labels, so you don't pick only the ones you think are foreign. Take a mix: 5 foods, 5 clothes or shoes, 5 machines, and 5 toys or school things.

materials.item: 20 things from around the home, chosen before reading their labels
a world map, printed or on a phone

experiments.safety: Read only labels on the outside of things or on boxes. Never open or turn over a plugged-in machine. Ask a grown-up to read the label on the back of a TV or fridge.

schedule.what: Pick 20 things. Guess. Read every label. Count, make a bar chart and mark the countries on a map.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Then draw a bar for each country, with the number of things made there.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: where 20 things were made

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home together and choose 20 things, without reading labels. 2. Take a mix of food, clothes, machines and toys.
flow.say: Let's choose 20 things before we look at any labels. If we look first, we might pick only the surprising ones.
flow.kid: Choose 20 things. Don't read the labels yet! Pick food, clothes, machines and toys.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Made Where survey. You choose 20 things from your home before reading their labels.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: Out of these 20, how many do you think were made in India? Why?
flow.kid: Guess: how many of the 20 were made in India? Why do you think so?

ask.q: Why did you guess that number?
good: Food is made near us.
Phones and toys often come from far away.
Any reason is good.

flow.do: 1. Find the label on each thing: 'Made in', 'Country of origin', or 'Manufactured by' with an address. 2. Write the exact words in the table.
flow.say: Now be a label detective. Look for 'Made in' or 'Country of origin'. Write the words exactly as they are.
flow.kid: Find the label on each thing. Look for Made in or Country of origin. Write it down.
flow.parent: Packets of food list a 'Manufactured by' address, which shows the city. Phones and machines may say 'Made in India' or 'Assembled in India'. That means the parts may have come from elsewhere. Clothes have a small cloth label inside the collar or seam. Some things have no label at all. Write 'no label'.

flow.do: 1. Count how many things came from each country. 2. Draw a bar chart. 3. Mark each country on the map.
flow.say: Let's count. How many from India? From each other country? Now let's find them on the map.
flow.kid: Count the things from each country. Draw a bar for each. Find each country on the map.

check.q: A phone box says 'Made in India', but its parts came from five countries. What does the label tell you?
options: Where the phone was put together at the end
check.why: A 'Made in' label names the country where the thing was finished. The parts can come from many countries, and the design from another. Picking 'every part' is a common idea, but labels don't show the parts.

flow.do: Ask your child what they found, and what surprised them.
flow.say: What did you find? Which kind of thing came from furthest away? Why do you think trade lets a toy from far away cost less than one made nearby?
flow.kid: What did you find? What came from furthest away? What surprised you?

ask.q: Which kinds of things were mostly made in India?
good: Food.
Clothes.
Things that are heavy or go bad quickly.

flow.parent: Most families find food and clothes are Indian, while electronics and toys are a mix. Many phones sold in India are now put together in India. Any result is real.

activities.title: The Window Walk: what did public money give us today?

materials.item: a window or balcony with a view of the street, or a short walk to the gate

activities.safety: Stay on the balcony or at the gate with a grown-up. Don't lean out of windows.

schedule.what: Look out at the street and list everything that was paid for with public money.

activities.record: Write the list, and put a star next to the thing you think cost the most.

flow.do: 1. Stand at a window, a balcony or the gate. 2. Ask your child to name everything they can see that nobody in our family owns, but everyone uses.
flow.say: Look outside. What can you see that we don't own, but we all use?
flow.kid: Look outside. What do we all use, but nobody in our home owns? Make a list.
flow.parent: Good answers: the road, the footpath, the street light, the drain, the bus stop, a traffic signal, the garbage van, a park, a government school, the water pipe. Accept anything shared.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Window Walk. You look out at the street and list the shared things you can see.

flow.do: Ask who paid for each thing on the list.
flow.say: Who do you think paid for that street light? And the road?
flow.kid: Who paid for the street light? Who paid for the road? Guess.

good: The government.
The corporation.
All of us, with tax money.

flow.parent: Most children say 'the government'. That is right, and it's enough for now. The Bill Detective experiment will show where the government's money comes from.

flow.do: Leave your child with a question.
flow.say: The government paid. But where did the government get the money? Keep that question. We'll find out from our own bills.
flow.kid: The government paid. But where did it get the money? Keep that question!
flow.think: Where does the government get its money from?

activities.title: Is the School Allowed to Do This?

materials.item: this list of 8 situations, read aloud by a grown-up
two pieces of paper marked ALLOWED and NOT ALLOWED

schedule.what: Decide whether a school may do each thing, under the Right to Education Act.

activities.record: Write how many you got right, and the one that surprised you most.

flow.do: 1. Put the two papers on the floor, a few steps apart. 2. Explain the game.
flow.say: I will read what a school does. If the law allows it, jump to ALLOWED. If not, jump to NOT ALLOWED.
flow.kid: Listen to what the school does. Allowed? Jump there. Not allowed? Jump to the other paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of a jumping game about the Right to Education Act. You decide what a school may and may not do.

flow.do: Read each situation. Your child jumps, then you give the rule. 1. A school tests a 6-year-old before giving her a seat. 2. A government school gives free textbooks. 3. A school asks for a donation for a seat. 4. A school turns away a child with no birth certificate. 5. A private school keeps a quarter of its Class 1 seats for children from poor families. 6. A teacher hits a child for being late. 7. A government school serves a free lunch. 8. A child with a disability is given a seat in the nearby school.
flow.say: Ready? Here is the first one. Allowed, or not allowed?
flow.kid: Listen. Jump to allowed or not allowed. Then hear the rule.
flow.parent: Answers: 1 not allowed. 2 allowed. 3 not allowed. 4 not allowed. 5 allowed, and the law requires it. 6 not allowed: the Act bans hitting and frightening children. 7 allowed. 8 allowed: children with disabilities have the same right to a school place.

check.q: A school asks Farhan's father for a big donation before giving Farhan a seat in Class 1. Is that allowed?
options: Yes, if the school is private
No, the Right to Education Act does not allow donations for admission
check.why: The Right to Education Act bans asking for a donation, also called a capitation fee, for admission. This rule is for private schools too. The father agreeing does not make it allowed.

flow.do: Ask which rule surprised your child most.
flow.say: Which rule surprised you most? Why do you think the law needed to say it?
flow.kid: Which rule surprised you? Why do you think the law says it?

ask.q: Why do you think the law bans tests for small children?
good: So children aren't turned away for not knowing things yet.
School is where they learn, so they shouldn't need to know it first.

activities.title: The Muster Roll Check: be a social auditor

materials.item: the pretend muster roll and job cards below, copied onto paper by a grown-up
a pencil and a red pen

schedule.what: Compare a pretend muster roll with job cards and what villagers say, and find the mistakes.

activities.record: Write a short audit report: what is wrong, and what should happen next.

flow.do: 1. Copy this muster roll onto paper. Pond work, 5 days, Monday to Friday. Pushpa: 5 days. Gowri: 3 days. Kamala: 5 days. Suresh: 5 days. Saroja: 4 days. Muthu: 5 days. 2. Hand it to your child and ask if anything looks wrong.
flow.say: This is the attendance register from a pond-digging site. Read it. Does anything look wrong to you?
flow.kid: Read the register. Five days of pond digging. Does anything look wrong?
flow.parent: On its own, the register looks fine. Every number is between 0 and 5. That is the point: a record can look perfect and still be false.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Muster Roll Check. You read a pretend work register from a village pond.

flow.do: 1. Now give the job cards. Pushpa: 5 days. Gowri: 5 days. Kamala: 5 days. Saroja: 4 days. Muthu: 5 days. There is no job card for Suresh. 2. Give the villagers' two notes. Note 1 says Kamala was at her sister's wedding on Thursday and Friday. Note 2 says nobody in the village knows a worker called Suresh.
flow.say: Now you have more evidence: the job cards, and what the villagers say. Compare them with the register, name by name.
flow.kid: Now check each name. Compare the register, the job cards and the villagers' notes.
flow.parent: Your child should find three problems. Gowri worked 5 days but the register shows 3, so she is owed 2 days. Kamala is marked for 5 days but was away for 2. Suresh has no job card and nobody knows him, so he may be a fake worker.

flow.do: 1. Mark each problem in red. 2. Write a short audit report together.
flow.say: Mark each mistake in red. Then let's write the audit report. What is wrong, and what should happen now?
flow.kid: Mark each mistake in red. Write what is wrong. Write what should happen.

check.q: How did you find that Suresh might be a fake worker?
options: He had no job card, and nobody in the village knew him
check.why: The register alone looked fine. The mistake showed only when it was compared with other evidence: the job cards and what the villagers knew. That is what a social audit does.

flow.do: Ask the last question.
flow.say: Who gets the money paid for a worker who doesn't exist? Why does reading the register aloud in the village help?
flow.kid: Who gets the money for a fake worker? Why does reading the list aloud help?

ask.q: Why does reading the register aloud help?
good: The workers know their own days.
The villagers know who really worked.
It's harder to cheat when everyone can check.

activities.title: Write a Practice RTI Letter

materials.item: a real local question about public money or a public service

activities.safety: The parent decides whether to send it, and their name goes on it, not the child's. Never write a child's phone number or address on anything you share.

schedule.what: Choose a real question about your area, and write it as a Right to Information application.

activities.record: Keep the letter. If you send it, mark 30 days on a calendar.

flow.do: 1. Think of one real question about your area together. 2. Write it down in plain words.
flow.say: Is there something near us that you wonder about? A broken road, a park, a school, a bus stop? Let's turn it into one clear question.
flow.kid: Think of something near home you wonder about. A road? A park? Make it one clear question.
flow.parent: Good questions ask for facts that are written down somewhere. For example: 'How much money was spent on repairing the road outside our school in the last year, and who did the work?' A question like 'Why is the government so slow?' cannot be answered with a record.
flow.context: This is the first step of writing a practice RTI letter. You choose a real question about your area.

flow.do: Write the letter together. 1. To: The Public Information Officer, and the office's name and address. 2. Subject: Application under the Right to Information Act, 2005. 3. The questions, numbered. 4. The parent's name, address and the date. 5. A line saying the fee is paid.
flow.say: Every RTI letter has the same parts. Let's write ours, part by part. Keep each question short.
flow.kid: Write it part by part. Who is it to? What is the subject? Then number your questions.
flow.parent: You don't have to give a reason for asking. For a central government office, you can apply online at rtionline.gov.in and pay 10 rupees. For state and city offices, check the state's RTI rules for the fee and how to pay.

flow.do: Read the letter back, and check each question.
flow.say: Let's read it like the officer would. Is each question clear enough that they know exactly what to send?
flow.kid: Read it like the officer. Is each question clear? Fix any that are fuzzy.

check.q: Which question is best for an RTI letter?
options: Why is our road always so bad?
How much was spent on repairing Gandhi Road in 2025, and which company did the work?
Can you please be nicer to us?
check.why: An RTI question asks for information that is written in records. The cost of the repair and the company's name are in the office's files. 'Why is it always bad' is an opinion, and being nicer is a wish. Neither is information the officer can copy and send.

activities.title: Ask an Elder: what did school cost you?

schedule.what: Interview an elder about going to school when they were 8.

activities.record: Write their answers, and one thing that is different for you now.

flow.do: Write five questions together. 1. How far was your school? 2. Did you pay fees? 3. Was there lunch at school? 4. Did all the children you knew go to school? 5. Did girls and boys go the same number of years?
flow.say: Let's ask a grandparent, an older relative or a neighbour what school was like when they were your age. Let's write the questions first.
flow.kid: Write five questions for an elder. How far was school? Did you pay? Was there lunch?
flow.context: This is the first step of an interview. You ask a grandparent or older neighbour about going to school when they were small.

flow.do: 1. Call or visit the elder. 2. Your child asks the questions. 3. Write short answers.
flow.say: Ask your questions slowly, and listen carefully. You can ask 'Why?' after any answer.
flow.kid: Ask each question. Listen. Write a few words for each answer. Ask why!
flow.parent: Many grandparents, especially grandmothers, will say they left school early or never went. Let that sink in, without making the elder feel judged. Thank them at the end.

flow.do: Compare their answers with your child's school today.
flow.say: What is different for you now? Which law do you think made the biggest difference?
flow.kid: What is different for you now? Which law helped most?

good: School is free now.
There is lunch at school.
Girls go to school as much as boys.
Every child aged 6 to 14 has a right to school.

setup.caption: 1. Call or visit an elder with your questions.

setup.art: A notebook page with two columns: 'An elder at 8' and 'Me at 8'.
setup.caption: 2. Write their answers, and compare them with your school today.

projects.title: A Week of Bills: how much tax does our family pay?
projects.context: This is a one-week project. Every day you add the day's bills to an envelope. At the end of the week, you add up how much tax your family paid.

materials.item: a large envelope or a plastic folder
all the printed bills the family gets for 7 days, including online order invoices

schedule.what: Make a Tax Envelope. Draw a table in the notebook: Day, Bill, Tax. Add today's bills.
Add today's bills, and write their tax in the table.
Add the bills from days 3 and 4.
Add the bills from days 5 and 6.
Add the last bills. Add up the week's tax. Make a list of what that money could help pay for.

projects.record: The table of the week's bills, the total tax, and a drawing of one shared thing the tax helps pay for.

flow.do: 1. Label an envelope 'Tax Envelope'. 2. Draw a table with three columns: Day, Bill, Tax. 3. Add today's bills and fill in the table.
flow.say: For one week, we will save every bill. At the end, we'll see how much tax our family paid in seven days.
flow.kid: Make a Tax Envelope. Draw a table. Day, Bill, Tax. Add today's bills.
flow.parent: Online orders have an invoice in the app, usually under 'Order details'. Read the tax from the phone, then write it in the table. A grown-up should cover card numbers before the child handles bills.
flow.context: This is the first step of A Week of Bills. You set up an envelope to collect a week of bills.

flow.do: Each day or two, add the new bills and write their tax.
flow.say: Any new bills today? Let's find the tax and write it in.
flow.kid: Any new bills? Find the GST. Write it in the table.
flow.wait: Add bills again every day or two, until day 7.

flow.do: 1. On day 7, add up the tax column. 2. Round to the nearest 10 rupees. 3. Talk about how many families live in your building, and how much they might pay together.
flow.say: Let's add up our week. If every family in our building paid about the same, how much would that be?
flow.kid: Add up the tax for the week. How much did our family pay? Now think about every family in the building.

ask.q: If 40 families each paid about the same, how much would that be?
good: 40 times our total.
A lot more than one family's.

flow.parent: Most city families find a few hundred rupees of GST in a week. Multiplying by the families in a building shows how small amounts add up. Use rounded numbers to keep the sum easy.

challenges.title: A Notice Board Everyone Can Read
challenges.problem: A village is building a new pond. The law says the work's details must be shown in public. But some villagers cannot read, and others read only Telugu. Design a notice board that tells everyone what is being built, what it costs, who is working, and how to complain.
constraints: It must make sense to someone who cannot read.
It must fit on one sheet of chart paper or the back of a calendar.
It must show at least the cost, the start and end dates, and who to complain to.
materials: chart paper or the back of an old calendar
general: Paint the work's details on a wall at the site, which many government works do.
Show the cost in rupee notes drawn in rows, so the size of the number can be seen.
Read the board aloud at a village meeting every week.
creative: Use pictures for each worker, such as a drawing of their face, with a tick for each day worked.
Draw a phone with the complaint number in large digits, since many people who cannot read can read numbers.
Make a calendar of the work with a picture for each week: digging, lining, filling with water.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own board. Show it to someone in the family who has not seen it, and ask them to tell you what it says without reading any words.

flow.do: Read the problem together, and ask what a person who cannot read needs.
flow.say: Imagine a grandmother in the village who cannot read walks past the pond. How could a board tell her what is going on?
flow.kid: Imagine someone who can't read. How could a board tell them about the pond?
flow.context: This is the first step of a design challenge. You make a notice board about public work that everyone can understand.

flow.do: Draw three quick ideas before choosing one.
flow.say: Designers try many ideas first. Draw three quick ideas, in a few lines each.
flow.kid: Draw three quick ideas. Just a few lines each.

flow.do: 1. Make the best idea on chart paper. 2. Test it: ask a family member to explain it without reading the words.
flow.say: Make your best idea. Then let's test it. Can someone understand it without reading?
flow.kid: Make your board. Ask someone to explain it without reading the words.
flow.parent: Cover the words with your hand when you test it, to check the pictures alone say enough.

flow.do: Read the usual and creative solutions together, then improve your board.
flow.say: Here's what others have tried. Which idea would you add to yours?
flow.kid: Read the other ideas. Which one would make your board better?

challenges.title: The Register That Is Hard to Fake
challenges.problem: In the Muster Roll Check, a false name and false days were written into the register. Design a way of keeping attendance at a work site that is very hard to fake.
constraints: It must work in a village with no internet.
A worker who cannot read must be able to check their own record.
materials: an ink pad or a little turmeric paste for thumbprints
general: Each worker puts their thumbprint against their name every day.
Read the register aloud to all the workers at the end of each week.
Give each worker a job card that is stamped each day, so there are two records to compare.
creative: Take one group photo of all the workers each day, with the date written on a slate in the photo.
Pay wages straight into each worker's own bank account, so money can't go to a made-up name.
Pin a copy of the register at the tea shop, where everyone sees it.
challenges.your_turn: Now invent your own register. Try it with your family for three days, for something like who watered the plants. Then try to cheat it. Could you?

flow.do: Remind your child how the cheating worked in the Muster Roll Check.
flow.say: Remember the pretend register with a worker called Suresh, whom nobody knew? How did the cheat get in?
flow.kid: Remember the fake worker Suresh? How did the cheat get into the register?
flow.context: This is the first step of a design challenge. You invent a work register that is hard to fake.

flow.do: 1. Draw a new kind of register. 2. Try it for a family job, such as who watered the plants today.
flow.say: Design a register that would catch a fake name. Then let's try it at home.
flow.kid: Design your register. Try it at home. Who watered the plants today?
flow.parent: If you use turmeric paste for thumbprints, it stains, so keep a damp cloth ready. An ink pad from a stationery shop is cleaner.

flow.do: 1. Try to cheat your own register. 2. Read the usual and creative solutions. 3. Improve the design.
flow.say: Now try to cheat it. Could you add a fake name, or a fake day? What would stop you?
flow.kid: Now try to cheat it! Could you add a fake name? What stops you?

quiz.p: Tara, a girl in Hyderabad, buys a packet of biscuits. Does she pay any tax?
quiz.why: Yes. GST is added to the price of packaged food, so she pays a little tax inside the price, even though she never hands money to the government.
opts: Yes, a little GST is in the price
Only if she has a job
Only if the shop is big

quiz.p: A family's bill shows CGST 9% and SGST 9%. How many rupees of tax are on every 100 rupees of price?
quiz.why: The two are added: 9 + 9 = 18 rupees in every 100.
A right is something every person may have or do, which the law protects. It is not a gift that can be taken back.
opts: Something every person may have or do, which the law protects
A present from a rich person

quiz.p: Which of these is a right that India's laws give?
quiz.why: Every child aged 6 to 14 has the right to a free school place. The others are not rights.
opts: A free school place for children aged 6 to 14

quiz.p: Revathi is 6 and wants to join Class 1. A school says she must pass a test first. Is that allowed?
quiz.why: No. The Right to Education Act bans tests for small children before admission.
opts: No, the Right to Education Act does not allow it
Only if she is a girl

quiz.p: Up to which class does the Right to Education Act promise free school?
quiz.why: It covers ages 6 to 14, usually Class 1 to Class 8.

quiz.p: Why may any citizen ask how public money is spent?
quiz.why: Public money comes mostly from tax that people pay, so it is the people's money.
opts: Because it came mostly from the people, as tax
Because only rich people pay tax
Because it is a school rule

quiz.p: To whom do you send a Right to Information letter?
quiz.why: Every government office has a Public Information Officer whose job is to answer these letters.

quiz.p: Under the rural job guarantee, where does a village family ask for work?
quiz.why: The Gram Panchayat is the elected village council. It registers families and gives job cards.

quiz.p: At a social audit, what happens?
quiz.why: The work records are read aloud to the village, and the workers say whether they are true.
opts: The pond is filled with water
Officers check the sums in secret
Work records are read aloud, and workers say if they are true

quiz.p: Divya checks 20 things at home. Her phone says 'Made in India', and her shoes say 'Made in Vietnam'. What does this show?
quiz.why: Things in one home come from many countries. Countries trade, and this is part of globalisation.
opts: Her home has things from more than one country
Shoes can't be made in India

quiz.p: Which is a real worry about trade with the whole world?
quiz.why: Cheaper goods from far away can put some local makers, such as handloom weavers or toy makers, out of work.
opts: Some local makers lose their work

quiz.p: Some people say officers get too many RTI letters. Others say the letters catch waste. What is the fairest thing to say?
quiz.why: Both sides have real points. A fair answer weighs the time taken against the waste caught.
opts: Both have a point, and the evidence matters

items.p: Jaya, a girl in Class 3 in Coimbatore, sees 'GST' on her family's supermarket bill. What is GST?
items.why: GST is the Goods and Services Tax, added to the price of most things we buy. The shop passes it on to the government. A strong answer knows it is tax, not a shop charge or a discount.
opts: Tax that goes to the government

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 3 in Vijayawada, says, 'Only rich people pay tax.' Is Arjun right?
items.why: False. GST is in the price of most things anyone buys, so a family buying soap and oil pays tax too. Rich people also pay income tax, but almost everyone pays GST.

items.p: A restaurant bill shows CGST 2.5% and SGST 2.5%. So every 100 rupees of price has ____ rupees of tax added.
items.why: Add the two rates: 2.5 and 2.5 make 5. So 5 rupees of tax are added to every 100 rupees of price.

items.p: Kavya, a girl in Chennai, looks around her street. Sort each thing: paid for with public money, or owned by one family?
items.a: see items
items.why: The road, street light, drain, bus stop and government school are shared, and paid for with public money. The sofa, the fridge and a bicycle belong to one family. A strong answer asks: 'Can everyone use it?'

items.p: Match each law or word to what it means.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four come up all through the unit. A strong answer can give an example of each.
pairs: free school for every child aged 6 to 14
any citizen may ask a government office for information
paid work for village families who ask for it
tax added to the price of things we buy

items.p: Nandini, aged 9, is kept at home to look after her baby brother instead of going to school. Which law says she has a right to go?
items.why: The Right to Education Act gives every child aged 6 to 14 the right to free school. The other laws are about information and work.

items.p: A government school gives Nisha her textbooks free. Her mother says, 'Nothing is really free.' What does she mean?
items.a: A strong answer: the books were paid for with public money, which comes mostly from tax that families like Nisha's pay when they shop.
items.why: This is the heart of the unit. The school does not charge, but the money came from everyone, through tax.

items.p: To ask a question under the Right to Information Act, you must explain why you want to know.
items.why: False. The law says nobody has to give a reason. The information belongs to the public.

items.p: Selvi writes an RTI letter to the city office about a broken street light. How long does the office have to reply?
items.why: The office must reply within 30 days. If the question is about someone's life or freedom, it must reply within 48 hours.

items.p: Draw three things on or near your street that were paid for with public money. Label each one.
items.a: Any three shared things, such as a road, a street light and a bus stop, each labelled.
items.why: A strong drawing shows things everyone can use, not things one family owns.

items.p: At a village meeting, the work register is read aloud. Who knows best whether it is true?
items.why: The workers know how many days they really worked. That is why the register is read to them. An officer far away can check only that the sums add up.
opts: An officer in the city office
The workers named in the register

items.p: Divya and her brother Kiran, in Mysuru, play The Shared Pot game. The pot can pay for only one more thing.
items.a: A strong answer picks one, gives a reason based on who it helps and how many people, and then fairly states the other side's best point.
items.why: There is no single right answer. Real governments make this choice every year. Good reasoning thinks about who needs it most and how many people it helps.

views.says: Spend it on school lunch. Hungry children can't learn, and some families can't afford lunch.
Spend it on street lights. Everyone uses the street at night, and dark roads are not safe.

items.ask: Whose choice do you agree with? Give a reason. Then say the best point the other one made.

items.p: Under the Right to Education Act, school is free for every child aged 6 to ____.
items.why: Free and compulsory school is for ages 6 to 14, which is usually Class 1 to Class 8.

items.p: Put the parts of an RTI letter in order, from top to bottom.
a: To: The Public Information Officer, and the office's address
Subject: Application under the Right to Information Act, 2005
The name, address and date of the person asking
items.why: The letter says who it is for, then what it is, then the questions, and last who is asking.
items: The name, address and date of the person asking
To: The Public Information Officer, and the office's address
Subject: Application under the Right to Information Act, 2005

items.p: In the Bill Detective, which of your bills had the most tax in every 100 rupees? Why do you think it had more than the others?
items.a: A strong answer names the bill and its rate from the table, and suggests a reason, such as food carrying less tax than plastic goods or machines.
items.why: This uses the child's own evidence. Food and medicines mostly carry 5%, many other goods 18%, and fresh vegetables none.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out? The road, the street light, the government hospital, our family's car.
items.a: our family's car
items.why: The car belongs to one family. The others are shared and paid for with public money.

items.p: Imran, a boy in Class 4 in Kochi, reads 'Assembled in India' on his family's new phone box. What does that tell him?
items.why: Assembled means put together. The parts may have been made in other countries, then joined in a factory in India.
opts: Every part was made in India
The phone was designed in India
The parts were joined together in India
The phone will only work in India

items.p: Choose two things from your Made Where survey. Where was each one made? Why do you think it came from there?
items.a: A strong answer names the things and countries from the child's own table, and gives a reason, such as 'food goes bad, so it is made nearby' or 'that country has many toy factories'.
items.why: This uses the child's own evidence. Any reason that thinks about cost, distance or what goes bad is good.

items.p: A private school in Bengaluru must keep a quarter of its Class 1 seats for children from poor families.
items.why: True. The Right to Education Act says private schools keep 25% of seats in their first class for children from weaker and disadvantaged families. The government pays the school for these seats.

items.p: Ramu lives in a village. He asked the Gram Panchayat for work 20 days ago, and got none. What does the job guarantee law say?
items.why: If no work is given within 15 days of asking, the family must be paid an unemployment allowance. That is why it matters to get a dated receipt when you ask.
opts: He must move to the city
He must be paid an allowance

items.p: Sort each question: can it be asked under the Right to Information Act?
items.a: see items
items.why: Records about public money and public services can be asked for. A private person's money or marks, and secrets that would harm the country's safety, can be kept back.
items: How much did the road repair cost?
How much money is in my neighbour's bank account?
How many teachers does our government school have?
Where are the army's secret plans?
When will the broken street light be fixed?
What marks did my friend get?

items.p: Why is a social audit held in front of the whole village, and not inside an office?
items.a: A strong answer: the workers and villagers know the truth about who worked and what was built, so they can catch false entries that look fine on paper.
items.why: Records can look correct and still be false. Only the people they are about can check them.

items.p: Match each person to what they did.
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these people helped make a right real for ordinary families.
pairs: opened a school for girls in Pune in 1848
helped lead public hearings in Rajasthan where work records were read aloud
spread free school lunches across Madras State in the 1950s
helped write the rural job guarantee law

items.p: The rural job guarantee's first work began in 2006 in Bandlapalli village, in ____ district of Andhra Pradesh.
items.why: Prime Minister Manmohan Singh launched it there on 2 February 2006.

items.p: A wooden toy is made in Channapatna, near Bengaluru. A plastic toy is made in a giant factory far away. Why might the far-away toy cost less?
items.why: Giant factories make huge numbers of the same thing, so each one costs little to make. Big ships carry them cheaply. A strong answer sees that distance is not the only thing that sets a price.
opts: The factory makes huge numbers, and ships carry them cheaply

items.p: From 1 July 2026, India's new rural job law promises up to 125 days of paid work a year to each village family.
items.why: True. The VB-G RAM G Act replaced MGNREGA from that date. MGNREGA had promised up to 100 days.

items.p: A shop in Kanchipuram sells handloom silk saris and cheap machine-made saris.
items.a: A strong answer picks a view, uses a fact from the unit, and gives the other side's best point fairly.
items.why: Both are real views. Trade has made cloth cheaper, and it has also cost many handloom weavers their work.

views.says: Each of my saris takes me days to weave. When people buy cheap machine-made saris, weavers like me lose our work.
I can buy three machine-made saris for the price of one handloom sari. My family's money has to stretch.
Cheap cloth helps millions of families. But the government can help weavers, for example by helping them sell to buyers far away.

items.ask: Which view is closest to yours? Give one reason. Then say one thing another person has right.

items.p: In the story The Name on the List, Ratnamma is a grandmother who digs a farm pond. Draw her job card. Show that she worked 15 days in April, and the wages she was paid.
items.a: A drawing of a small booklet with her name, a table of dates or days, and a wage column.
items.why: A job card is the worker's own record. A strong drawing shows the days worked, so it can be compared with the register.

items.p: Put the steps of a social audit in order.
a: The audit team copies the work records
The records are read aloud, name by name
Workers say whether each entry is true
Mistakes are written down and sent to the officers
items.why: First the records are collected, then read to the people they are about, then corrected.
items: Workers say whether each entry is true
Mistakes are written down and sent to the officers
The audit team copies the work records
The records are read aloud, name by name

items.p: A register of work looks neat, and every sum adds up. What is the best way to check that it is true?
items.why: Neat sums show only that the numbers agree with each other. Comparing with job cards and asking the workers checks them against what really happened.
opts: Compare it with the job cards and ask the workers
Ask the person who wrote it

items.p: Draw a simple shop bill. Label these parts: the total, CGST, SGST and the tax rate.
items.a: A drawn bill with the four parts labelled.
items.why: Knowing where these are lets anyone find the tax on their own bills.

items.p: Government schools give a free cooked lunch. Why might a free lunch bring more children to school?
items.a: A strong answer: children from poor families get a meal they might not get at home, so families send them, and fed children learn better.
items.why: Studies in India have found more children, especially girls, come to school when lunch is served.

worksheets.title: Fair or Not? Big Questions about Rights (challenge)

items.p: A rich family and a poor family both buy the same soap and pay the same tax on it. Is that fair? Explain your thinking.
items.a: A strong answer sees both sides: the tax is the same in rupees, but it is a much bigger part of a poor family's money. That is one reason richer people also pay income tax.
items.why: GST is the same rate for everyone, so poorer families spend a bigger share of their money on it. People argue about this.

items.p: Two people argue about the Right to Information Act.
items.a: A strong answer chooses a side, gives a reason, and answers back from the other view fairly.
items.why: Both points are real. Answering takes time, and openness also catches waste.

views.who: Mrs Rao, an officer in a town office
views.says: I answer forty RTI letters a month. Some ask for thousands of pages for no good reason. It leaves less time for my real work.

views.who: Ms Nair, a citizen in Kochi
views.says: My RTI letter showed that our road was paid for twice. Without it, nobody would have found out.

items.ask: Whose side are you on? Give a reason. Then say how the other person might answer you.

items.p: Parvathi, a woman who works on a village pond, was paid for 12 days but worked 15. Which record would help her most at the social audit?
items.why: Her own job card shows the days she really worked. Comparing it with the register shows the mistake.

items.p: A village school has a building but no teacher. Does the right to education still help the children there? What would you do?
items.a: A strong answer says the right is not real without a teacher, and suggests using it: writing to the education office, or asking under RTI why no teacher was sent.
items.why: A right needs people to do the work it promises. The law gives families a way to demand it.

items.p: In the Bill Detective, a plastic bucket had 18 rupees of tax for every 100 rupees of price. The bucket's price before tax was 200 rupees. How much tax was added?
items.why: 18 rupees for each 100. 200 is two hundreds, so 18 + 18 = 36 rupees.

items.p: A 'Made in' label tells you where every part of the thing was made.
items.why: False. It names where the thing was finished. A phone or a shirt can have parts or cloth from many countries.

items.p: Arjun, the boy in Class 3 from Vijayawada, says something else. Find the mistake in his thinking: 'The government pays for the road with its own money, not ours.'
items.a: A strong answer: the government's money comes mostly from tax that people pay, so the road was paid for with our money.
items.why: The government holds public money for everyone. It does not make its own money from nothing.

items.p: Which of these would be the best evidence that the job guarantee helped poor families?
items.why: A careful study compares families with and without the work, and measures something real, such as meals. A speech or one story can't show how common something is.
opts: A minister's speech saying it worked
A study comparing how many meals families ate in villages with and without the work

items.p: Make a picture poster for families who cannot read. It should tell them that every child aged 6 to 14 has a free school place.
items.a: A poster that a person who cannot read could understand: a child, a school, the numbers 6 and 14, and a sign that it costs nothing.
items.why: Good design uses pictures and numbers, since many people who cannot read words can read numbers.

items.p: Sort each one: a good side of world trade, or a worry about it.
items.a: see items
items.why: Real trade has both. A strong answer can explain why each one belongs where it is.
items: ships and planes burn a lot of fuel
foods from many countries to try

items.p: Gandhi asked Indians to buy swadeshi, things made close to home. A wooden Channapatna toy costs 300 rupees and a plastic toy from far away costs 100. What would Gandhi say? What would you choose, and why?
items.a: A strong answer says Gandhi would choose the local toy to support local makers, and then gives the child's own reasoned choice, with one fact about price, makers or fuel.
items.why: There is no single right answer. The question is about weighing money against the maker's work and the cost of carrying things far.

items.p: Muniyamma, a woman in a village in Tamil Nadu, asks the Gram Panchayat for work and gets a dated receipt. Why does the receipt matter?
items.why: If no work comes within 15 days, the receipt proves when she asked, so Muniyamma can claim the allowance.
opts: It proves when she asked, so she can claim the allowance if no work comes

open_questions.q: How much do social audits and open records really reduce cheating?
open_questions.why_open: Many studies find they help, but they are hard to measure, because hidden cheating is hidden. Results differ from state to state.

open_questions.q: Who gains most from trade with the whole world, and who loses?

open_questions.q: What is the fairest way to collect tax?

open_questions.q: How can a right be made real where there are too few teachers, doctors or officers?
open_questions.why_open: A law can promise a right, but it needs people and money to keep it. Nobody has found a perfect way.
