maths.problem: In the Bill Detective, a packet of biscuits and some oil cost 400 rupees before tax. The tax was 5 rupees for every 100 rupees. How much tax was added, and what was the total?
maths.answer: 20 rupees of tax. The total was 420 rupees.
maths.explain: 400 is four hundreds. Each hundred has 5 rupees of tax, so 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 rupees. The total is 400 + 20 = 420 rupees.
maths.context: This is about the Bill Detective, where you find the tax on your family's bills.
maths.why_maths: Working out the tax yourself lets you check that a bill is right, and see how much of the price goes to the government.

maths.problem: Under the new rural job law, a village family can get up to 125 days of work a year. Suppose the wage is 300 rupees a day. How much could the family earn in a year?
maths.explain: Split 125 into 100 and 25. 100 days at 300 rupees is 30,000 rupees. 25 days at 300 rupees is 7,500 rupees. 30,000 + 7,500 = 37,500 rupees. Real wages are set for each state every year, so 300 is a practice number.
maths.context: This is about the rural job guarantee, which promises paid work to village families.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows what a promise of days really means for a family's money, and lets us compare the old 100 days with the new 125.

maths.problem: In the Made Where survey, Kavya found 12 things made in India, 5 in China, 1 in Vietnam and 2 with no label. How many more things were made in India than in all other countries together?
maths.explain: Other countries: 5 + 1 = 6. India: 12. 12 - 6 = 6. So 6 more were made in India. The 2 with no label are not counted, because we don't know where they were made.
maths.context: This is about the Made Where survey, where you check 20 things at home for a 'Made in' label.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which country made most of our things. Comparing bars tells us whether our home depends more on India or on the rest of the world.

maths.problem: Selvi posts an RTI letter on 5 March. The office must reply within 30 days. By what date must the answer come?
maths.explain: March has 31 days. From 5 March to 31 March is 26 days. 4 more days reach 4 April. 26 + 4 = 30.
maths.context: This is about the Right to Information Act, which says an office must answer within 30 days.
maths.why_maths: Counting days on a calendar tells you exactly when the office is late, so you know when you may appeal.

maths.problem: In A Week of Bills, one family paid about 300 rupees of GST in a week. Their building has 40 families. If each paid about the same, how much tax would the building pay in a week?
maths.explain: 40 families times 300 rupees. 4 times 3 is 12, so 40 times 300 is 12,000. That is about 12,000 rupees in one week, from one building.
maths.context: This is about A Week of Bills, where you add up the tax your family pays in seven days.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying shows how small amounts from many families add up to a big shared sum, which is how public money is built.

roots.context: We have found the tax on our own bills and learned the rights it pays for. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Nearly every bill you checked had GST on it, even small ones. So almost every family that shops pays tax, yours too. That tax pays for 'free' school books, roads and street lights. So the government spends money that belongs to all of us together.
deep_truth.habit: We say 'government money' and call school books and lunches 'free', as if the money came from nowhere. But it was collected a few rupees at a time from almost every family's shopping. 'Free' only means everyone has already paid.
deep_truth.evidence: The Bill Detective: the GST lines on the family's own supermarket, restaurant and medical shop bills. Only loose fresh food or a tiny shop's handwritten slip had none.

three.who_am_i: You are a taxpayer already. Every packet of biscuits you buy puts a few rupees into the shared purse.
three.what_is_life: Life in a country is shared. Your road, your school and your lunch were paid for by families you will never meet, and you help pay for theirs.
three.what_is_this_world: A world where strangers pool their money to build things for everyone, and then have the right to ask how it was spent.

roots.thread: One family's GST on one bill is a few rupees. Crores of families shopping every day pour those rupees into one shared purse. That one purse then becomes many things: a pond in Anantapur, a lunch in Madurai, a street light in Kochi. Many small payments become one, and the one becomes many shared things again. That is why every one of those families has a right to see the accounts.

teachings.teaching: Let the ruler look into the work of his officers every day. When they do not go wrong, the world does not go wrong.
teachings.link: This couplet was written in Tamil about 2,000 years ago, and it asks for daily checking of the people who handle public work. A social audit and an RTI letter are ways for ordinary people to do that checking today.

teachings.teaching: Ashoka ordered that reports on the people's affairs be brought to him at any hour, whether he was eating, resting or travelling, so that he could deal with them at once.
teachings.link: A ruler who wants to hear the people's problems at any time is close to the idea behind the Right to Information Act: the people's business should not be hidden or delayed.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if in a city flat today. The Bill Detective needs 5 printed bills. Most families have supermarket, restaurant or medical shop bills, and online order invoices can be read on the phone. A handwritten kirana slip usually shows no GST, which is a real result, not a failure. Bills can carry card and phone numbers, so a grown-up covers them first. Percent is not taught: the child adds the two printed rates, such as 2.5 and 2.5, or 9 and 9. The Made Where survey asks the family to choose 20 things before reading labels, so the sample is fair. Food packets show a 'Manufactured by' address instead of a 'Made in' line. The Window Walk works from a balcony or the building gate. The Muster Roll Check has its full data in the steps, so the parent needs no preparation beyond copying it. The RTI letter is practice: the parent decides whether to send it, with their own name. Turmeric paste stains, so the challenge suggests an ink pad. Both games work with one parent and one child. The spine is about 85 minutes.

how_we_found_out.story: In the early 1990s, workers in the villages of central Rajasthan were often paid less than the minimum wage on government work sites. Officials said the records showed everyone had been paid in full. Those records were kept in offices, and villagers were not allowed to see them. Most people believed that official records, signed and stamped, must be true. A group called the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan, or MKSS, set out to check. It had been started in 1990 by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey, Shankar Singh and others. In 1994 and 1995, they got copies of bills and muster rolls and read them aloud at village public hearings, called jan sunwai. Workers stood up and said, 'I never got this money.' Some names belonged to people who had died or moved away. Some works on paper had never been built. The records were not the truth. Their slogan was 'Hamara paisa, hamara hisaab': our money, our accounts. Their campaign helped bring Rajasthan's right to information law in 2000, and the Right to Information Act for all of India in 2005.
how_we_found_out.who: The MKSS, started by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey, Shankar Singh and others, and the workers of central Rajasthan
how_we_found_out.when: 1990 (MKSS begins), 1994 and 1995 (the first public hearings), 2000 (Rajasthan's law), 2005 (the Right to Information Act)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: People believed that signed and stamped government records must be true, and that ordinary people had no need to see them. When the records were read aloud to the workers, many entries turned out to be false.
